rows.explanation: Change B adds a 60s in-memory cache to GET /api/tags and invalidates it only when articles are created (in articlesCreate). Concrete scenario: create article with tag 'solo', GET /api/tags (cached), delete the article (tag deleted), GET /api/tags still lists 'solo'. A's integration test queries prisma directly, so it doesn't catch this.

After merging, the password is hashed twice: bcrypt(bcrypt(newPassword)) is stored. Login compares the plaintext against the stored hash, so a user who changes their password through POST /api/user/password can no longer log in with the new password. B's own test only checks the stored value is not plain text and differs from the old hash, so it still passes, and A's test covers only PUT /api/user. Neither change does this alone: A's @updatedAt only fires on real edits since nothing else updated articles, and B's view increment only touched views when updatedAt was manual. rows.explanation: A caches the tag list and invalidates the cache via a prisma.$use middleware on writes to Tag or Article models. B adds, after deleting an article, a prisma.tag.deleteMany to remove orphan tags. Walking through the merge: article.delete triggers the middleware (model Article, action delete), which sets cache = null after the delete completes. Then B's tag.deleteMany runs, which also triggers the middleware (model Tag, action deleteMany), setting cache = null again after that delete completes. Both invalidations occur after their respective writes, so the cache is cleared after the orphan tag removal. A concurrent getTags call between the two writes could repopulate the cache with stale tags (including orphans) after the first invalidation, but the second invalidation (after deleteMany) clears it again. So the final state is consistent. The one remaining race is a read that started before the deleteMany completed and finishes caching after the invalidation, but that is a generic race in A's design, not something B introduces specifically. The changes are complementary, not duplicates.

With after=Y, the filter keeps only articles with updatedAt < Y.updatedAt, which excludes X, so X is skipped. Conversely, after=X returns Y, which was already shown, causing duplicates. rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes hashPassword and compareWithHash trim whitespace before bcrypt operations, so passwords are normalized by trimming at both registration and login. Change B adds a confirm-password endpoint that calls bcrypt.compareSync directly on the raw (untrimmed) password, deliberately bypassing compareWithHash (to avoid its logging). Once A's trimming is merged, any user whose registered password has leading/trailing whitespace (e.g. '  secret ') has a stored hash of 'secret'. Login works with ' secret ' via compareWithHash, but the confirm-password endpoint compares the raw '  secret ' against the hash and returns 403. Conversely, a password that was stored untrimmed pre-A would fail login but pass confirm. This is a concrete inconsistency: B relies on the assumption that bcrypt.compareSync(raw, user.password) is equivalent to the app's password check, which A breaks. B's own tests pass since they use passwords without whitespace.

That regression comes entirely from A's change to hashing and affects login on its own, so it is not a conflict created by the merge. B's confirm-password endpoint behaves the same way as login. B's integration tests use plain passwords without whitespace. A's logging additions are independent of B's controller. No duplicated or contradictory logic exists between the two changes.

The middleware fires after the article.delete call, setting cache = null, and again on tag.deleteMany since model is Tag and action deleteMany is in WRITE_ACTIONS. Both calls complete before the delete handler returns, so no stale cache window exists (a concurrent getTags read between them could cache pre-cleanup tags, but the later deleteMany invalidates again unless it was no-op; even then, the middleware still nulls the cache after next() returns). So the cache is correctly invalidated after orphan tag cleanup. No duplicate intent either: caching vs orphan cleanup are different problems.

rows.explanation: Both changes address the problem of passwords being stored unhashed. Change A fixes the existing PUT /api/user path by hashing inside userUpdatePrisma. Change B adds a separate POST /api/user/password endpoint that hashes the new password in the controller before calling userSetPasswordPrisma. B's endpoint also doesn't pass through userUpdatePrisma, so there is no double hashing, and runtime behavior is correct. But the merged code now has two independent ways to change a password: PUT /api/user with a password field (guarded by no current-password check), and POST /api/user/password (which verifies the current password). This duplicates the password-change feature, and the new endpoint's security check can be bypassed via the PUT route. The two paths hash in different layers, one in the DB helper and one in the controller, which is a contradictory design for the same problem.

A user who viewed an article before it was renamed loses it from their recent list; viewing it again under the new slug adds a new row. The ordering key and the cursor key no longer match. Concrete scenario: article X was created early but edited recently (high updatedAt, low createdAt). With ?after=X, the filter keeps articles whose updatedAt is older than X's updatedAt, so articles newer by createdAt than X (that were not edited recently) are returned again, while articles created before X but edited after X's updatedAt are skipped. Pagination therefore duplicates or drops items. B's own test passes only because both createdAt and updatedAt are monotonic there. Change A intended ordering by creation time, and B's cursor assumes ordering by updatedAt.

rows.label: conflict

Merged: a user who registers with a password containing leading/trailing whitespace (e.g. " secret ") has the hash of "secret" stored. Login via compareWithHash trims and succeeds, but confirm-password compares the raw " secret " and returns 403 for the correct password. Similarly, a user who types "secret " when confirming gets 403 even though login would accept it. B's confirm endpoint relied on the stored hash matching the raw password, which A's trimming breaks, and B's direct bcrypt call skips A's trimming, causing inconsistent password verification between login and confirm-password.

rows.label: conflict

Once merged, a user who registered with surrounding whitespace (e.g. '  secret ') has a stored hash of the trimmed value. Login (via compareWithHash) succeeds with either form, but confirm-password with the exact password the user typed at registration ('  secret ') fails with 403, because untrimmed input is compared against a hash of the trimmed value. Likewise, a user typing ' secret' passes login but fails confirmation. B's code was correct against the old hashing contract; A's change breaks the assumption that bcrypt.compareSync(rawPassword, storedHash) is equivalent to compareWithHash. Existing tests use passwords without whitespace, so they pass.

A's other changes are logging additions that don't interact with B. A normalizes in the controllers (login and register) via a new normalizeEmail helper, while B normalizes in the DB helpers (userCreatePrisma and userGetEmailPrisma) with inline trim().toLowerCase(). Merged, every email is normalized twice by two different implementations, so the normalization logic is duplicated and one of the two layers should be removed. Behavior is harmless since normalization is idempotent, but the intent is duplicated, and both sides even add near-identical integration tests.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes article renames actually change the slug (previously a bug where the slug stayed the same). Change B adds a RecentView table that stores article slugs as plain strings, with no foreign key to Article and no cascade. After A's fix, renaming an article changes its slug, but existing RecentView rows keep the old slug. In recentArticlesPrisma, views whose slug no longer matches an article are silently dropped via flatMap, so a renamed article disappears from users' recent lists, and orphan rows count toward the take: KEEP limit, so users can see fewer than 10 recents. Re-viewing under the new slug creates a duplicate view row only for the new slug, and the old row lingers. Neither change alone causes this: before A, slugs never changed, so B's slug-as-key assumption held.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: After merge, articlesListPrisma orders by createdAt desc (Change A) but the new ?after= cursor filters on updatedAt < cursor.updatedAt (Change B). The sort key and the cursor key no longer match. Concrete scenario: article X is created first but edited recently (updatedAt late), Y created later but never edited. Order by createdAt desc is [Y, X]. With ?after=Y, before = Y.updatedAt (early); X.updatedAt is later than that, so X is excluded and the page skips it. Conversely, articles that appear earlier in the list can reappear on the next page. B's own test (which sets updatedAt only) would still pass because createdAt order is then insertion order, matching updatedAt order, but real-world edited articles break pagination.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A adds an https-only image rule to userUpdateValidator, which guards PUT /api/user. Change B adds a new endpoint PUT /api/user/image that sets the same image field but is not routed through userUpdateValidator, so it accepts any string (e.g. http://, arbitrary text) with no https check. In the merged code, the image rule that A introduces can be bypassed via B's endpoint: PUT /api/user rejects 'http://x' while PUT /api/user/image accepts it and persists it via userUpdatePrisma. The invariant 'image must be an https URL' is no longer enforced for all image updates. B's existing tests do not catch this since they only use https URLs.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes add a way for the current authenticated user to list their favorited articles: A adds a new GET /api/user/favorites endpoint, and B adds a ?favorited=me shortcut on GET /api/articles. Each is correct and runs without error alongside the other, but they solve the same problem in two different ways. Their integration tests even have identical setups and assertions. The merged code now has two API surfaces for the same feature, and one of them should be removed.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes tag names stored lowercase and trimmed, and makes the article list filter case-insensitive (it lowercases the query tag). Change B adds GET /api/tags/:tag, which looks up the tag with an exact, case-sensitive match on req.params.tag. Merged, the new endpoint disagrees with the list filter: GET /api/articles?tag=REACT finds the tag, but GET /api/tags/React returns 404 because the stored name is 'react'. The mismatch comes from B relying on exact-match lookup while A changes the tag storage and matching semantics. It is a minor inconsistency rather than data corruption, and B's own tests (lowercase names) pass.

Change B only trims comment bodies in commentCreatePrisma. The only link is createComment (A, logging only) calling commentCreatePrisma (B); A's addition there is purely logging and doesn't interact with the trimming. The tag normalization and comment trimming are unrelated concerns, so they don't duplicate or contradict each other and both work correctly together.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes slugfy keep accented and non-Latin letters (e.g. 'crème-brûlée', 'привет-мир'). Change B restricts the GET /api/articles/:slug route to /[a-z0-9-]+/, returning 404 for anything else. Merged, any article created with an accented or non-Latin title gets a slug that GET /api/articles/:slug can no longer serve, since the route pattern rejects those characters. A's own new test creates 'Crème Brûlée' and the slug is 'crème-brûlée', which B's route would 404 on. B's assumption (slugs are ASCII lowercase/digits/dashes) was true before A, and A breaks it. The other routes (PUT, DELETE, favorites, comments) still use plain /:slug, so the system becomes inconsistent: the articles can be created and edited but not fetched.

They touch different validators for different resources (comments vs. articles) with independent constants and independent tests. Neither relies on assumptions the other breaks, and they do not duplicate the same fix; they are two separate, complementary validation additions.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes address overly long article titles but in different layers with different limits: A rejects titles over 100 chars at validation (400), B silently truncates titles over 120 chars at save time. Runtime is consistent: since the validator rejects >100, B's truncation (at 120) never triggers via the API, so it becomes dead code on the HTTP path. Nothing breaks, but both solve the same problem (title length limiting) with contradictory policies (reject vs. truncate) and inconsistent thresholds (100 vs 120), so one should be removed or the limits unified.

rows.label: conflict

B adds GET /api/tags/:tag, which looks up the tag by exact req.params.tag. In the merged code, all stored tags are lowercase, but getTag does not apply the same normalization. A request like GET /api/tags/React returns 404 even though the tag 'react' exists, while GET /api/articles?tag=REACT works. This is a concrete inconsistency: B's lookup relies on the stored tagName matching the URL param exactly, which A's change breaks for mixed-case input. B's own tests use lowercase tags, so they pass.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A removes the email from the JWT payload in createUserToken (token now only has user.username). Change B's isModerator reads req.auth?.user?.email from that token and returns false when email is missing. After merge, tokens never contain email, so isModerator always returns false and the moderator deletion feature silently never works (moderators fall back to author-only deletion). Neither change alone breaks this: B alone works with email in tokens; A alone has no consumer of the email claim. The merged deleteComment passes isModerator(req) which is always false.

B's isModerator reads only req.auth.user.username from the token and matches against MODERATOR_USERNAMES, so it does not depend on the email claim. B's isModerator unit test builds requests with email but never goes through createUserToken. The deleteComment edits (logging in A, isModerator argument in B) are in different regions and compose cleanly. The logging additions do not affect B's behavior. No concrete runtime or intent conflict.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes hashPassword and compareWithHash trim passwords, so registration hashes the trimmed password and login compares the trimmed input. Change B adds a confirm-password endpoint that calls bcrypt.compareSync directly on the raw, untrimmed password, deliberately bypassing compareWithHash. After merging, a user who registers with a password containing surrounding whitespace (e.g. '  secret ') gets the hash of 'secret'. Login with the same raw password works, because compareWithHash trims it. The confirm-password endpoint then compares '  secret ' against the hash of 'secret' and returns 403 for the correct password. B's integration tests use whitespace-free passwords, so they still pass. Both changes are individually correct, but A's change to the password-normalization assumption breaks B's endpoint, which bypasses the shared helper. This is a runtime inconsistency created by the combination.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes hashPassword and compareWithHash trim whitespace before bcrypt. Change B's userConfirmPassword calls compareWithHash(password, user.password), so it simply gets the trimmed comparison. B's tests use registerUser, which goes through the register controller's hashPassword (also trimmed), so hash and compare stay consistent. One edge case: a whitespace-only password passes B's truthiness check but trims to empty, and compares against a stored hash of an empty string, which is the same behavior as login. Existing stored hashes of passwords with leading or trailing whitespace would no longer match, but that is a standalone regression in A, not a combination issue with B. A's other changes are logging additions with no interaction. No concrete failure scenario arises from the merge.

Change B's isModerator reads req.auth?.user?.email from the token to decide moderator status, returning false when email is missing. In the merged code, tokens issued after A no longer contain email, so isModerator always returns false and moderators can never delete others' comments. B's own isModerator unit test passes because it fakes a request with email, and existing tests pass, but real moderator behavior silently breaks. Neither change alone has this problem.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes hashPassword and compareWithHash trim passwords before hashing and comparing, so registration and login both operate on trimmed passwords. Change B adds userConfirmPassword, which deliberately bypasses compareWithHash (to avoid its logging) and calls bcrypt.compareSync(password, user.password) with the raw, untrimmed password. After the merge, a user whose password was registered with surrounding whitespace (e.g. ' secret ') has a stored hash of 'secret'. Login via compareWithHash trims the input and works with either form, but confirm-password with ' secret ' compares the untrimmed input against the hash of 'secret' and returns 403. Conversely, a user who registers with 'secret' and later confirms with ' secret ' (copy and paste with whitespace) is rejected, although login would accept it. A's own test explicitly asserts that whitespace variants must match, so B's endpoint contradicts that invariant by bypassing the shared helper. Neither change alone has this inconsistency.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes hashPassword and compareWithHash trim passwords (so registration and login operate on trimmed values). Change B adds a confirm-password endpoint that deliberately bypasses compareWithHash and calls bcrypt.compareSync(password, user.password) with the raw, untrimmed password. Merged, a user who registered with a password containing leading/trailing whitespace (e.g. '  secret ') has a stored hash of the trimmed value 'secret'. Login succeeds with either form, but confirm-password with the original '  secret ' returns 403 because the raw string is compared against the hash of the trimmed string. Likewise a user whose password was hashed trimmed, entering a copy-paste with stray whitespace, passes login but fails confirm-password. B's own tests use passwords without whitespace so they still pass. This breaks A's new invariant that password comparison ignores surrounding whitespace, so the two endpoints now behave inconsistently.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes hashPassword and compareWithHash trim the password before hashing/comparing. Change B adds a confirm-password endpoint that calls compareWithHash(password, user.password) against the stored hash. Since the trim is symmetric (applied on both hash and compare in the shared helpers), the new endpoint just inherits the trimmed-comparison behavior, matching login. Users registered before A's change with leading or trailing whitespace in their password would fail both login and confirm equally, so there is no divergence between the two. The remaining A changes are logging additions that do not affect B's controller. B does not duplicate any of A's work.
